category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Course of the Posterior Division Branches
statement: Which of the following vessels ascends across the pelvic inlet and is located posterior to the external iliac vessels and the psoas muscle?
optionExplanations: The inferior vesical artery is a branch of the anterior division in males that supplies the bladder base and prostate; it does not ascend across the inlet.
The iliolumbar artery is a branch of the posterior division that travels superiorly and laterally, passing deep to the psoas and external iliac vessels to reach the iliac fossa.
The umbilical artery runs forward from the anterior division along the lateral pelvic wall toward the anterior abdominal wall.
The lateral sacral arteries descend along the anterior sacral foramina on the posterior pelvic wall; they do not ascend across the pelvic inlet.
The superior gluteal artery is the continuation of the posterior division that passes backward between the lumbosacral trunk and S1 to exit the pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Iliolumbar artery: this artery ascends across the pelvic inlet posterior to the external iliac vessels, psoas, and iliacus muscles.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Tributaries of the prostatic venous plexus
statement: The prostatic venous plexus is a critical structure during pelvic surgery. Which vessel is a major tributary that enters this plexus after passing under the pubic symphysis?
options: Deep dorsal vein of the penis
correctOption: Deep dorsal vein of the penis
optionExplanations: The internal pudendal vein is the vessel that the prostatic plexus eventually drains toward, but it is not a tributary entering the plexus from the penis.
The inferior rectal vein drains into the internal pudendal vein, not the prostatic plexus.
The deep dorsal vein of the penis passes between the pubic symphysis and the perineal membrane to reach the prostatic venous plexus.
The obturator vein typically drains directly into the internal iliac vein along the lateral pelvic wall.
The external pudendal vein is a superficial vessel draining the skin of the penis and scrotum, eventually joining the femoral vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The prostatic plexus receives the deep dorsal vein of the penis and numerous vesical veins and drains into the internal iliac veins.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Course and Transition of the External Iliac Artery
statement: Which specific path and transition does the external iliac artery follow as it descends toward the lower limb?
options: It runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis following the sacral curve.
It ascends across the pelvic inlet posterior to the psoas major muscle.
It passes through the greater sciatic foramen to enter the gluteal region.
It pierces the pelvic diaphragm to enter the perineum via the pudendal canal.
It follows the pelvic brim and passes under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.
correctOption: It follows the pelvic brim and passes under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.
optionExplanations: The external iliac artery is a vessel of the false pelvis following the pelvic brim; it does not follow the sacral curve of the posterior pelvic wall.
The iliolumbar artery, a branch of the internal iliac, ascends across the pelvic inlet; the external iliac artery descends along it and is medial, not posterior, to the psoas muscle.
Branches of the internal iliac artery, such as the superior and inferior gluteal arteries, pass through the greater sciatic foramen, not the external iliac artery.
The internal pudendal artery, not the external iliac, relates to the pudendal canal in the perineum.

The external iliac artery follows the pelvic brim along the medial psoas border. Its transition from the pelvic cavity to the lower limb occurs precisely as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament, where its name changes to the femoral artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac artery runs along the medial border of the psoas muscle, following the pelvic brim (see Fig. 8.10), and gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches. It leaves the false pelvis by passing under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A 65-year-old male undergoes surgery for a large rectal tumor. The surgeon observes that the chief vein draining the mucous membrane of the upper rectum is dilated. This vessel eventually drains into which system?
options: The internal iliac vein and the systemic circulation
The renal vein and the systemic circulation
The inferior mesenteric vein and the portal circulation
The external iliac vein and the systemic circulation
The median sacral vein and the common iliac system
correctOption: The inferior mesenteric vein and the portal circulation
optionExplanations: The internal iliac vein receives the middle rectal vein, not the superior rectal vein which drains the upper mucosa.
The renal vein receives gonadal drainage (on the left) but not rectal drainage.
The superior rectal vein is the primary drainage for the rectal mucosa and is the direct systemic-to-portal link, emptying into the inferior mesenteric vein.
The external iliac vein drains the limb and abdominal wall and has no role in rectal mucosal drainage.
The median sacral vein drains the posterior pelvic wall and enters the left common iliac vein, not the rectal mucosa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior rectal vein is a tributary of the portal circulation and drains into the inferior mesenteric vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: During a pelvic lymphadenectomy for suspected metastatic spread, a surgeon identifies the common iliac nodes. What is the standard anatomical 'step' for tracing the drainage of these nodes?
options: Tracing them posteriorly to the sacral hiatus
Tracing them medially to the internal rectal nodes
Tracing them inferiorly to the superficial inguinal nodes
Tracing them laterally to the femoral nodes
Tracing them superiorly to the para-aortic nodes
correctOption: Tracing them superiorly to the para-aortic nodes
optionExplanations: The sacral hiatus is an opening in the sacrum for anesthesia; it is not a destination for the common iliac lymphatic chain.
There is no major chain of internal rectal nodes that receive drainage from the common iliac chain; the drainage is generally ascending.
Superficial inguinal nodes drain the skin of the perineum and lower anal canal; they drain 'up' to the external iliac nodes, not down from the common iliac.
Femoral nodes are synonymous with deep inguinal nodes; they are inferior to the iliac chain in the lymphatic hierarchy.
In the pelvis, lymph nodes follow the arterial supply. Common iliac nodes receive drainage from internal and external iliac nodes and drain superiorly into the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The nodes are named after the blood vessels with which they are associated. Thus, there are external iliac nodes, internal iliac nodes, and common iliac nodes.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: An elderly patient with known prostate cancer presents with new-onset back pain. Radiographs show osteoblastic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae. Which venous pathway most likely facilitated this spread?
options: Prostatic venous plexus to the vertebral veins via valveless connections
Testicular vein to the renal vein
Superior rectal vein to the portal vein
External iliac vein to the inferior vena cava
Internal pudendal vein to the femoral vein
correctOption: Prostatic venous plexus to the vertebral veins via valveless connections
optionExplanations: The prostatic venous plexus is valveless and has direct communications with the Batson venous plexus (vertebral veins). Increased abdominal pressure (coughing/straining) can force cancer cells into the vertebral system.
The testicular vein is not the primary drainage for the prostate gland.
The superior rectal vein leads to the portal system and the liver; it would result in hepatic, not vertebral, metastases.
Drainage via the external iliac to the IVC would likely lead to pulmonary metastases as the next capillary bed is in the lungs.
The internal pudendal vein drains systemic blood from the perineum but does not provide a direct low-resistance path to the vertebrae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins... it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins. This explains the frequent occurrence of skeletal metastases in the lower vertebral column and pelvic bones

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a left-sided varicocele. Anatomically, why is the left testicular vein more susceptible to this condition than the right testicular vein?
options: The left testicular vein has more valves than the right
The left testicular vein joins the internal iliac vein
The left testicular vein joins the low-pressure inferior vena cava
The left testicular vein is shorter than the right
The left testicular vein joins the high-pressure left renal vein
correctOption: The left testicular vein joins the high-pressure left renal vein
optionExplanations: The number of valves is not the primary anatomical reason cited for the prevalence of left-sided varicoceles; the drainage site is the key factor.
Testicular veins do not drain into the internal iliac vein; they are abdominal drainage structures despite passing through the inguinal canal.
Joining the low-pressure IVC is the characteristic of the right testicular vein, which explains why right-sided varicoceles are rarer.
The left testicular vein is actually slightly longer than the right because it must ascend higher to reach the left renal vein.
The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle. The higher pressure in the renal vein and the mechanical disadvantage of the entry angle impede drainage, leading to varicocele.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": This is thought to be because the right testicular vein joins the low-pressure inferior vena cava, whereas the left vein joins the left renal vein, in which the venous pressure is higher.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: In the venous-arterial loop of the pelvis, the common iliac vein is formed by the union of the internal and external iliac veins. This union occurs specifically:
options: In front of the sacroiliac joint
Lateral to the common iliac artery
correctOption: In front of the sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein runs along the medial side of the external iliac artery, but the 'union' site is defined by the joint landmark.
Mirroring the arterial division, the venous union that forms the common iliac vein occurs in front of the sacroiliac joint.
L1 is the level for the renal veins and the termination of the testicular/ovarian veins, not the common iliac union.
Behind the inguinal ligament, the femoral vein becomes the external iliac vein; it has not yet joined the internal iliac vein.
The common iliac vein is typically medial and posterior to the common iliac artery as it ascends toward the IVC.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It [Internal iliac vein] passes upward in front of the sacroiliac joint and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein (see Fig. 8.10).

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: A patient has a blockage in the common iliac artery. Considering its course and branching, which vessel would remain patent if blood was supplied via retrograde flow from the femoral artery?
optionExplanations: The aorta is proximal to the common iliac; retrograde flow from the femoral would reach the external iliac first.
Superior suprarenal arteries are branches of the inferior phrenic arteries, unrelated to the iliac bifurcation.
The femoral artery is the direct continuation of the external iliac artery; thus, they share the same continuous vascular channel distal to the common iliac bifurcation.
The celiac trunk is an upper abdominal vessel completely independent of the iliac system.
The inferior mesenteric artery is a proximal branch of the aorta and not part of the common iliac's distal terminal system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac artery... leaves the false pelvis by passing under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: Which branch of the internal iliac artery is considered the functional homologue of the inferior vesical artery in the male?
optionExplanations: The vaginal artery occupies the same relative position and provides similar distribution to the bladder base as the male inferior vesical artery.
The internal pudendal artery is present in both sexes to supply the perineum and external genitalia.
The middle rectal artery exists in both males and females to supply the lower rectum.
The obturator artery exists in both sexes and follows the same course through the obturator canal.
The uterine artery is specific to females but is not the homologue of the inferior vesical artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Vaginal artery: this artery usually takes the place of the inferior vesical artery present in the male.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A patient with advanced portal hypertension secondary to cirrhosis presents with bright red blood per rectum. Examination reveals varicosities at the anorectal junction. Which systemic pelvic vein is participating in this portal-systemic anastomosis?
optionExplanations: The IVC is the ultimate termination of the systemic return but is not the specific vessel anastomodising at the rectal wall.
The external iliac vein does not receive tributaries from the rectum.
The deep circumflex iliac vein drains the lower abdominal wall into the external iliac vein.
The testicular vein is a systemic vein but has no involvement in the rectal portal-systemic anastomosis.
The middle rectal vein (and inferior rectal vein) are systemic vessels draining into the internal iliac system. They anastomose with the superior rectal vein (portal system) in the anal canal wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior rectal vein is a tributary of the portal circulation and drains into the inferior mesenteric vein. The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins, respectively. The union between the rectal veins forms an important anorectal portal–systemic anastomosis.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A surgeon operating on the pelvic floor must identify the prostatic venous plexus. Where is this plexus located, and what is its primary clinical significance regarding hemorrhage?
options: Located in the deep perineal pouch; drains the superficial dorsal vein
Located in the retrorectal space; communicates with the portal system
Located between the bladder neck and the base of the prostate; drains into the IVC
Located outside the prostatic capsule; possesses thin walls and no valves
Located within the prostatic parenchyma; causes arterial bleeding
correctOption: Located outside the prostatic capsule; possesses thin walls and no valves
optionExplanations: It receives the deep dorsal vein of the penis, but the plexus itself is a pelvic (not perineal) structure.
It is related to the rectum anteriorly but is separated by the rectovesical septum and has no significant portal communication unlike the rectal veins.
It drains into the internal iliac veins, not directly into the IVC.
The plexus lies between the true and false capsules of the prostate. Its thin, valveless walls make it a significant source of profuse bleeding during prostatectomy.
The plexus is periprostatic (outside the capsule), and bleeding from it is venous, not arterial.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The veins form the prostatic venous plexus, which lies outside the capsule of the prostate... The veins have thin walls, are valveless, and are drained by several large trunks directly into the internal iliac veins. Damage to these veins can result in a severe hemorrhage.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Course of the Internal Pudendal Artery
statement: A patient presents with a deep abscess in the ischioanal fossa. During surgical drainage, the clinician must avoid the pudendal canal. The internal pudendal artery, which travels in this canal, reached this location by which sequence of structures?
options: Greater sciatic foramen, passing above the piriformis, then the inguinal ligament
Obturator canal, then the lesser sciatic foramen
Lesser sciatic foramen, then the greater sciatic foramen into the gluteal region
Pelvic inlet, passing lateral to the psoas, then the femoral canal
Greater sciatic foramen, curling around the ischial spine, then the lesser sciatic foramen
correctOption: Greater sciatic foramen, curling around the ischial spine, then the lesser sciatic foramen
optionExplanations: Passing above the piriformis is characteristic of the superior gluteal artery, not the internal pudendal.
The obturator canal transmits the obturator artery, not the internal pudendal artery.
This reverses the sequence; the artery leaves the pelvis via the greater foramen and enters the perineum via the lesser.
This describes the path of the external iliac artery toward the thigh, not a branch of the internal iliac.
The internal pudendal artery follows an 'out-and-in' course: out via the greater sciatic foramen, around the ischial spine, and back in via the lesser sciatic foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Internal pudendal artery: this artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and enters the gluteal region below the piriformis muscle (see Fig. 8.10). It then curls around the ischial spine (with the pudendal nerve) and enters the perineum by passing through the lesser sciatic foramen.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Branches of the External Iliac Artery
statement: The external iliac artery gives off only two branches before passing into the thigh. These branches are essential for providing collateral circulation. What are they?
options: Inferior epigastric and Deep circumflex iliac
correctOption: Inferior epigastric and Deep circumflex iliac
optionExplanations: Iliolumbar and lateral sacral are branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.
The external iliac is a relatively simple vessel, yielding only the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac before exiting the pelvis.
Vesical arteries are visceral branches arising from the internal iliac artery.
Gluteal arteries are branches of the internal iliac artery (superior from posterior division, inferior from anterior).
Obturator and umbilical are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac artery... gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches. It leaves the false pelvis by passing under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Where does the right ovarian vein typically drain?
optionExplanations: While many pelvic organs drain into the internal iliac vein, the ovaries (and testes) retain their embryonic drainage to the high posterior abdominal wall vessels.
The right renal vein does not typically receive the ovarian vein; the right ovarian vein enters the IVC directly.
The left renal vein receives the left ovarian vein, not the right one.
The common iliac vein is formed by iliac vessels and does not receive the gonadal veins.
The right gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava on the right side and into the left renal vein on the left side. This is the same relationship as the testicular veins in males.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Drainage of the median sacral vein
statement: Which specific pelvic vein does the median sacral vein join at its termination?
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein is primarily for lower limb drainage and does not receive the median sacral vein.
The median sacral vein is a small parietal vein that follows the median sacral artery and typically terminates in the left common iliac vein.
The text explicitly identifies the left common iliac vein as the destination, likely due to the asymmetry of the common iliac veins.
The right common iliac and left common iliac veins join to form the IVC, but the median sacral vein joins the left common iliac before this formation.
The internal iliac vein receives lateral sacral veins, but the median one goes to the common iliac.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median sacral veins accompany the corresponding artery and end by joining the left common iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
coreConcept: Posterior Relations of the Iliac Termination
statement: A patient with a suspected pelvic mass requires evaluation of the pelvic inlet. If a tumor originates from the tissues immediately posterior to the common iliac artery's termination, which joint is most likely to be directly involved?
optionExplanations: The symphysis pubis is an anterior midline structure; the common iliac arteries are posterior pelvic vessels.
The sacroiliac joint is the immediate posterior relation to the point where the common iliac artery bifurcates into the internal and external iliac arteries at the pelvic inlet.
The hip joint is lateral and inferior to the common iliac termination; the external iliac artery passes toward it but is separated by the psoas.
The lumbosacral joint (L5-S1) is superior and more medial to the termination point at the sacroiliac joint.
The sacrococcygeal joint is far inferior to the pelvic inlet where the common iliac ends.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Transition of the pampiniform plexus to the testicular vein
statement: An extensive venous network known as the pampiniform plexus emerges from the posterior border of the testis. Which of the following describes the correct mechanistic transition of this plexus as it ascends toward the abdominal cavity?
options: It forms a single testicular vein at the level of the deep inguinal ring
It remains a plexus until it drains directly into the inferior vena cava
It bifurcates into the internal and external testicular veins at the inguinal canal
It reduces in size to form a single testicular vein at the superficial inguinal ring
It joins the vesical venous plexus before entering the internal iliac vein
correctOption: It forms a single testicular vein at the level of the deep inguinal ring
optionExplanations: The multiple small veins of the pampiniform plexus coalesce into a single testicular vein at the internal (deep) inguinal ring before ascending on the posterior abdominal wall.
The plexus must consolidate into a single vessel before reaching its final abdominal drainage point.
There is no such anatomical division as internal or external testicular veins in the standard course of these vessels.
The plexus is still present within the inguinal canal; the reduction to a single vein occurs at the deep ring, not the superficial ring.
The testicular veins do not drain into the vesical plexus or the internal iliac vein; they follow a specific abdominal route.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": As the plexus ascends, it becomes reduced in size so that at about the level of the deep inguinal ring, a single testicular vein is formed.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: A 58-year-old male is diagnosed with a tumor involving the mucous membrane of the upper rectum. Which vessel is the chief source of blood supply to this specific area and represents the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery?
optionExplanations: The middle rectal artery is a small branch of the internal iliac that primarily supplies the muscular coat of the rectum rather than the chief mucous membrane supply.
The superior rectal artery is the primary supply to the rectal mucosa; its origin is the inferior mesenteric artery, which changes its name upon crossing the common iliac artery.
The external iliac artery supplies the lower limb and abdominal wall; it does not contribute to the visceral supply of the rectum.
The inferior rectal artery is a branch of the internal pudendal artery (from the internal iliac) and supplies the lower half of the anal canal.
The internal iliac artery provides the middle rectal branch, but it is not the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior rectal artery is a direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery. The name changes as the latter artery crosses the common iliac artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of Prostatic Venous Plexus
statement: A patient with prostate carcinoma develops secondary skeletal deposits in the lower vertebral column and skull. What specific characteristic of the prostatic venous plexus facilitates this metastatic pathway?
options: The plexus drains directly into the inferior mesenteric vein
The plexus contains high-pressure valves that force blood upward
The plexus has valveless connections with the vertebral veins
The plexus is situated within the thick fibrous capsule of the prostate
The plexus communicates with the portal system via the superior rectal vein
correctOption: The plexus has valveless connections with the vertebral veins
optionExplanations: The prostatic venous plexus drains into the internal iliac veins, not the inferior mesenteric vein.
The prostatic venous plexus is described as valveless; high-pressure valves are not present.

Because the veins are valveless and communicate with the vertebral venous system, changes in intra-abdominal pressure can cause blood to flow in a reverse direction, carrying malignant cells to the spine and skull.
The plexus actually lies outside the capsule of the prostate, though this does not explain the mechanism of distant metastasis.
The prostatic drainage is systemic (internal iliac), not portal. The superior rectal vein is the portal component of the anorectal junction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Cancer cells enter the skull via this route by floating up the valveless prostatic and vertebral veins.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Course of the Internal Pudendal Artery
statement: A surgeon is performing a perineal repair and needs to identify the internal pudendal artery as it enters the perineum. What is the correct anatomical course of this artery relative to the pelvic ligaments?
options: It passes through the lesser sciatic foramen and exits the perineum through the greater sciatic foramen.
It remains entirely intrapelvic until it pierces the pelvic diaphragm anteriorly.
It exits the pelvis via the obturator canal and travels along the ischiopubic ramus.
It travels deep to the sacrotuberous ligament and enters the pelvis via the sacral hiatus.
It passes through the greater sciatic foramen and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen by curling around the ischial spine.
correctOption: It passes through the greater sciatic foramen and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen by curling around the ischial spine.
optionExplanations: This reverses the sequence; the artery leaves the pelvis first through the greater sciatic foramen and enters the perineum second through the lesser.
The artery must exit the main pelvic cavity to reach the perineum and gluteal region; it is not strictly intrapelvic.
The obturator artery uses the obturator canal; the internal pudendal artery uses the sciatic foramina.
The sacral hiatus is a site for caudal anesthesia and transmits nerves, not the internal pudendal artery.

The internal pudendal artery has a complex course where it leaves the pelvis to enter the gluteal region (greater sciatic foramen), then immediately re-enters the perineum (lesser sciatic foramen) by wrapping around the ischial spine.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Internal pudendal artery: this artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen... It then curls around the ischial spine (with the pudendal nerve) and enters the perineum by passing through the lesser sciatic foramen.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Branches of the External Iliac Artery
statement: Which of the following arteries is characterized as a branch of the external iliac artery before it passes deep to the inguinal ligament?
optionExplanations: The iliolumbar artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, supplying the iliacus muscle and lumbar region.
The internal pudendal artery is a terminal branch of the internal iliac's anterior division and supplies the perineum.
The deep circumflex iliac artery, along with the inferior epigastric artery, are the only two significant branches arising from the external iliac artery in the pelvis.
The obturator artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, though its origin is famously variable (sometimes arising from the inferior epigastric).
The middle rectal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies the musculature of the lower rectum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac artery... gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches. It leaves the false pelvis by passing under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: What is the precise anatomical point where the external iliac vein commences its course in the pelvis?
options: At the level of the deep inguinal ring
At the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta
At the level of the second lumbar vertebra
In front of the sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia for the spermatic cord/round ligament; it is not the origin point of the external iliac vein.
The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta (at L4) marks the beginning of the common iliac arteries, not a venous origin point.
The external iliac vein is the direct continuation of the femoral vein as it passes deep to the inguinal ligament to enter the pelvis.
The second lumbar vertebra is the level of origin for the testicular and ovarian arteries, not the external iliac vein.
The area in front of the sacroiliac joint is where the internal and external iliac veins join to form the common iliac vein, rather than the origin of the external iliac vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac vein begins behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Contrast the drainage pattern of the median sacral veins with the standard pelvic venous tributaries.
options: They enter the portal circulation via the inferior mesenteric vein.
They drain into the right common iliac vein.
They end by joining the left common iliac vein.
They drain directly into the inferior vena cava at its bifurcation.
They accompany the internal iliac artery to join the internal iliac vein.
correctOption: They end by joining the left common iliac vein.
optionExplanations: The median sacral veins are part of the systemic venous system, not the portal system.
The median sacral veins specifically terminate on the left side, not the right.
Unlike many pelvic veins that correspond to arterial branches, the median sacral veins are unique in that they consistently drain into the left common iliac vein.
The IVC begins at L5 by the union of common iliac veins; the median sacral vein enters the common iliac vein just before this union.
The median sacral veins follow the median sacral artery, which originates at the aortic bifurcation, not the internal iliac system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median sacral veins accompany the corresponding artery and end by joining the left common iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: When contrasting the venous drainage of the anal canal to identify potential routes for portal-systemic anastomosis, which statement correctly identifies the termination of the superior rectal vein?
options: It drains into the internal iliac vein via the prostatic plexus.
It passes through the lesser sciatic foramen to join the femoral vein.
It is a systemic tributary draining into the internal pudendal vein.
It joins the middle rectal vein to empty into the external iliac vein.
It is a portal tributary draining into the inferior mesenteric vein.
correctOption: It is a portal tributary draining into the inferior mesenteric vein.
optionExplanations: The superior rectal vein belongs to the portal system, while the prostatic plexus drains into the internal iliac (systemic) system.
Rectal veins do not drain to the femoral vein; the inferior rectal vein follows the internal pudendal through the sciatic foramina to the internal iliac.
The internal pudendal vein receives the inferior rectal vein (systemic), not the superior rectal vein.
The middle rectal vein is systemic and drains into the internal iliac vein; it does not join the superior rectal vein's portal path, nor does any rectal vein drain to the external iliac.
The superior rectal vein is the primary drainage for the upper anal canal mucosa and is a direct tributary of the inferior mesenteric vein, which leads to the portal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior rectal vein is a tributary of the portal circulation and drains into the inferior mesenteric vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Which mechanistic pathway explains the drainage of the pampiniform plexus as it ascends toward the posterior abdominal wall?
options: It merges with the external iliac vein at the pelvic inlet.
It reduces to a single testicular vein at the level of the deep inguinal ring.
It remains as an extensive network until entering the inferior vena cava on both sides.
It bypasses the renal circulation to join the common iliac vein bilaterally.
It drains directly into the internal iliac vein via the vesical venous plexus.
correctOption: It reduces to a single testicular vein at the level of the deep inguinal ring.
optionExplanations: The testicular vein does not merge with the external iliac vein; it ascends on the posterior abdominal wall toward the IVC or left renal vein.
The pampiniform plexus is a network of veins that reduces to a single testicular vein as it leaves the inguinal canal and enters the abdominal cavity at the deep inguinal ring.
The plexus does not remain a network; it must consolidate into a single vessel before its final termination.
On the left side, the testicular vein specifically enters the renal vein, not bypassing the renal circulation.
The testicular veins do not drain into the internal iliac system; they follow a long course to the renal vein or IVC.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": As the plexus ascends, it becomes reduced in size so that at about the level of the deep inguinal ring, a single testicular vein is formed.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: A 70-year-old male with a history of atherosclerosis presents with acute onset of severe lower abdominal pain and a pulsatile mass at the level of the umbilicus. Imaging confirms an aneurysm at the bifurcation of the aorta. Which other vessel originates at this specific anatomical site along with the common iliac arteries?
optionExplanations: The median sacral artery is a midline branch arising exactly at the bifurcation where the aorta divides into the two common iliacs.
The testicular or ovarian arteries (gonadal) arise from the abdominal aorta at the level of the second lumbar vertebra.
The iliolumbar artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, arising distal to the common iliac bifurcation.
The superior rectal artery is the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, not a branch of the aortic bifurcation.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises higher up on the abdominal aorta, typically at the level of L3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median sacral artery is a small artery that arises at the bifurcation of the aorta.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Blood Supply to Male Internal Genital Organs
statement: A medical student is asked to trace the origin of the artery to the vas deferens in a male pelvis. Which vessel is the standard source of this branch?
optionExplanations: The iliolumbar artery supplies the iliacus, psoas, and quadratus lumborum muscles and is not involved in supplying the male reproductive tract.
The deep circumflex iliac artery is a branch of the external iliac artery and supplies the lower abdominal wall and iliac fossa, not the vas deferens.
The artery to the vas deferens usually arises from the superior vesical artery, which itself is a branch of the proximal patent part of the umbilical artery (anterior division).
The inferior epigastric artery is a branch of the external iliac artery; while it is related to the deep inguinal ring, it does not typically supply the ductus deferens.
The superior gluteal artery supplies the gluteal muscles and has no distribution to the pelvic viscera or internal genital organs.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Umbilical artery: the superior vesical artery arises from the proximal patent part of the umbilical artery. It supplies the upper portion of the bladder (see Fig. 8.10). It also gives off the artery to the vas deferens.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
coreConcept: Anatomic Termination of the Common Iliac Artery
statement: Where does the common iliac artery typically terminate by dividing into its terminal branches?
options: In front of the fourth lumbar vertebra
At the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen
At the level of the xiphoid process
At the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint
correctOption: At the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint
optionExplanations: While the common iliac arteries originate at the bifurcation of the aorta near L4, they do not terminate there; they course downward to the pelvic inlet.
The internal iliac artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions at the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen, not the common iliac.
The xiphoid process is an upper abdominal landmark; the common iliac artery is a lower abdominal/pelvic structure arising much lower from the aortic bifurcation.
The common iliac artery descends and reaches the pelvic brim (inlet) where it bifurcates in front of the sacroiliac joint into internal and external iliac branches.
The external iliac artery, not the common iliac, passes under the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Tributaries of the external iliac vein
statement: A surgeon performing a pelvic lymphadenectomy notes the tributaries of the external iliac vein. Which specific veins must be identified as they drain into the external iliac vein just proximal to the inguinal ligament?
options: Inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins
Median sacral and lateral sacral veins
correctOption: Inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins
optionExplanations: Uterine and vaginal venous plexuses drain into the internal iliac vein, not the external iliac vein.
The internal pudendal and obturator veins are typical tributaries of the internal iliac vein, corresponding to the branches of the internal iliac artery.
The superior rectal vein drains into the inferior mesenteric vein (portal system), while the middle rectal vein drains into the internal iliac vein.

The external iliac vein is a continuation of the femoral vein. Its primary tributaries within the false pelvis are the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins, which parallel their corresponding arteries.
The median sacral vein ends in the left common iliac vein, and lateral sacral veins typically drain into the internal iliac vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac vein... runs along the medial side of the corresponding artery and joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein (see Fig. 8.10). It receives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Which pelvic venous structure serves as the primary systemic component in the anorectal portal-systemic anastomosis?
options: Internal pudendal vein via the inferior rectal vein
correctOption: Internal pudendal vein via the inferior rectal vein
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein drains the lower limb and does not receive direct drainage from the rectal venous plexuses.
The testicular vein drains the gonads and does not participate in the anorectal venous anastomosis.
The inferior mesenteric vein is the continuation of the superior rectal vein and belongs entirely to the portal venous system.

The inferior rectal vein drains into the internal pudendal vein, which is a systemic tributary of the internal iliac vein. This connection allows blood to bypass the liver in cases of portal hypertension.
The superior rectal vein is the portal component of this anastomosis, draining ultimately into the liver via the portal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior rectal vein is a tributary of the portal circulation and drains into the inferior mesenteric vein. The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins, respectively. The union between the rectal veins forms an important anorectal portal–systemic anastomosis

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Which anatomical relationship is shared by both the testicular veins in males and the ovarian veins in females regarding their final drainage?
options: Both sets of veins drain into the vesical venous plexus.
Both left veins join the left renal vein.
Both left veins join the inferior vena cava at the level of L1.
Both right veins join the internal iliac vein.
Both right veins join the right renal vein.
correctOption: Both left veins join the left renal vein.
optionExplanations: The gonadal veins do not drain into the vesical plexus; they arise from the gonads and ascend the posterior abdominal wall.
Due to embryological development, both left testicular and left ovarian veins terminate in the left renal vein rather than the IVC.
The left veins join the renal vein; only the right veins join the IVC.
The right gonadal veins (testicular/ovarian) join the IVC directly, not the internal iliac vein.
The right gonadal vein enters the IVC, not the right renal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava on the right side and into the left renal vein on the left side. This is the same relationship as the testicular veins in males.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with chronic lower back pain and urinary hesitancy. Imaging reveals an aggressive prostatic carcinoma with osteoblastic metastases in the lumbar vertebrae. Labs show a PSA of 45 ng/mL. Which anatomical feature of the pelvic venous system facilitates the hematogenous spread of this cancer to the skeleton without passing through the lungs?
options: Shunting through the middle rectal vein into the portal circulation
Connections between the prostatic venous plexus and the valveless vertebral veins
Direct drainage of the prostatic plexus into the inferior vena cava
Communication between the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the iliolumbar veins
High-pressure reflux from the internal pudendal vein into the sacral veins
correctOption: Connections between the prostatic venous plexus and the valveless vertebral veins
optionExplanations: The middle rectal vein drains to the systemic system (internal iliac), and portal shunting would lead to liver, not spinal, metastases.

The valveless nature of the vertebral venous plexus (Batson's plexus) and its connections to the prostatic plexus allow cancer cells to migrate to the spine during fluctuations in intra-abdominal pressure.
The prostatic plexus drains into the internal iliac veins, not directly into the IVC.
The deep dorsal vein drains into the prostatic plexus, but it is the prostatic plexus's connection to the vertebral system that facilitates skeletal spread.
While the internal pudendal vein is related, the primary route for spinal metastasis is the direct communication with vertebral veins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins. During coughing and sneezing or abdominal straining, it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: Which vessel is described as the direct continuation of the umbilical artery's proximal patent segment?
optionExplanations: The uterine artery is a direct branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac, running across the pelvic floor.
The internal pudendal artery is a terminal branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac.
The umbilical artery is patent only proximally after birth; this patent section gives rise to the superior vesical artery which supplies the bladder.
The obturator artery is a separate branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac.
The inferior vesical artery is a separate branch, though it may occasionally arise with the middle rectal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Umbilical artery: the superior vesical artery arises from the proximal patent part of the umbilical artery.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
coreConcept: Regional Distribution of the Common Iliac Artery
statement: Which of the following best describes the anatomical distribution provided by the common iliac artery and its terminal branches?
options: It supplies the kidneys and the suprarenal glands
It exclusively supplies the abdominal viscera
It supplies the liver and the gallbladder
It supplies the pelvis and the lower limb
It exclusively supplies the thoracic diaphragm
correctOption: It supplies the pelvis and the lower limb
optionExplanations: The kidneys are supplied by the renal arteries, and suprarenals by superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from other sources.
Abdominal viscera are primarily supplied by the celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries.
The liver and gallbladder are supplied by the hepatic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk.
The common iliac artery is the primary trunk that bifurcates to supply both the pelvic cavity (internal iliac) and the lower extremity (external iliac).
The thoracic diaphragm is supplied by phrenic arteries, which are branches of the aorta or internal thoracic arteries.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The common iliac artery supplies blood to the pelvis and lower limb.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: Which artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery and ascends across the pelvic inlet posterior to the external iliac vessels?
optionExplanations: The superior gluteal artery is a branch of the posterior division but it exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis rather than ascending across the inlet.
The iliolumbar artery is the first branch of the posterior division. It turns upward to supply the iliac fossa and the psoas/iliacus muscles, passing behind the external iliac structures.
The deep circumflex iliac artery is a branch of the external iliac artery, not the internal iliac, and it runs along the iliac crest.
The lateral sacral arteries descend along the front of the sacrum and enter the sacral foramina; they do not ascend across the pelvic inlet.
The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division, not the posterior division, and it supplies the lower buttock region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Iliolumbar artery: this artery ascends across the pelvic inlet posterior to the external iliac vessels, psoas, and iliacus muscles.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: A 32-year-old female undergoes an emergency hysterectomy for severe postpartum hemorrhage. The surgeon decides to ligate the uterine artery near its origin. Which structure must the surgeon definitively identify and preserve as it passes inferior to the artery at the base of the broad ligament?
optionExplanations: The ureter runs 'under the bridge' formed by the uterine artery at the base of the broad ligament. Inadvertent ligation of the ureter is a classic surgical complication during hysterectomies.
The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring and is situated anterior and superior to the site where the uterine artery is typically ligated.
The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall in the obturator fossa and is not in the immediate vicinity of the uterine artery's crossing of the ureter.
The inferior vesical artery is the male homologue of the vaginal artery and is not found in the female pelvis; even its female counterpart (vaginal artery) is inferior to the uterine artery.
The internal pudendal nerve (pudendal nerve) exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen and is much more posterior and inferior to the broad ligament's base.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The uterine artery... crosses the ureter superiorly (see Chapter 9). It passes above the lateral fornix of the vagina to reach the uterus.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Termination of the median sacral vein
statement: During a dissection of the posterior pelvic wall, a surgeon identifies the median sacral veins. Where do these specific veins typically terminate?
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein receives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins, not the median sacral.
The median sacral veins consistently favor the left side for drainage, unlike many other midline structures.
The internal iliac veins receive most visceral tributaries, but the median sacral is an exception that joins the common iliac.
The IVC is formed by the union of the two common iliac veins; the median sacral vein joins one of its precursors.
The median sacral veins accompany the median sacral artery and drain specifically into the left common iliac vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The median sacral veins accompany the corresponding artery and end by joining the left common iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A patient with portal hypertension due to liver cirrhosis presents with bright red blood per rectum. Examination confirms internal hemorrhoids. Which specific venous transition explains the development of these varicosities?
options: Anastomosis between the superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal veins
Anastomosis between the inferior rectal and internal pudendal veins
Shunting from the median sacral vein to the left renal vein
Communication between the external iliac and internal iliac veins
Reflux from the inferior vena cava into the vesical plexus
correctOption: Anastomosis between the superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal veins
optionExplanations: The superior rectal vein is a portal tributary, while the middle and inferior rectal veins are systemic. Portal hypertension causes blood to shunt into the systemic rectal veins, leading to hemorrhoids.
The inferior rectal and internal pudendal veins are both systemic; their union does not involve the portal system.
There is no direct anatomical shunt between the median sacral and left renal veins mentioned in pelvic venous anatomy.
The union of external and internal iliac veins is a normal systemic pathway, not a site of portal-systemic collateral circulation.
The IVC and vesical plexus are both systemic; pressure here does not relate to portal hypertension directly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The union between the rectal veins forms an important anorectal portal-systemic anastomosis.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Origin and Course of the External Iliac Vein
statement: Which of the following describes the correct origin and initial course of the external iliac vein?
options: Begins at the pelvic brim as a continuation of the internal iliac vein
Begins behind the inguinal ligament and runs medial to the artery
Begins from the prostatic plexus and runs behind the psoas muscle
Begins at the sacroiliac joint and runs lateral to the artery
Begins as a continuation of the inferior epigastric vein
correctOption: Begins behind the inguinal ligament and runs medial to the artery
optionExplanations: It is a continuation of the femoral vein, not the internal iliac vein.
The external iliac vein is the direct superior continuation of the femoral vein once it passes deep to the inguinal ligament. Its position is medial to the external iliac artery.
The prostatic plexus drains into the internal iliac vein, not the external iliac vein.
The vein ends (joins the internal iliac) near the sacroiliac joint; it does not begin there.
The inferior epigastric vein is a tributary that drains into the external iliac vein, not its origin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac vein begins behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein. It runs along the medial side of the corresponding artery and joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: In the branching pattern of the common iliac artery system, which vessel is responsible for supplying the abdominal wall before leaving the pelvis?
optionExplanations: The internal iliac artery primarily supplies the pelvic viscera, perineum, pelvic walls, and buttocks, not the anterior abdominal wall.
The superior vesical artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery and supplies the upper portion of the urinary bladder.
The external iliac artery gives off branches like the inferior epigastric artery to the abdominal wall before becoming the femoral artery.
The obturator artery supplies the medial compartment of the thigh and pelvic walls, not the general abdominal wall.

The iliolumbar artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery; while it supplies the iliacus and psoas, the external iliac is the primary source for the abdominal wall via its branches.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac artery supplies the abdominal wall and lower limb.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: Which artery, arising from the internal iliac's posterior division, is noted for ascending across the pelvic inlet posterior to the external iliac vessels and the psoas muscle?
optionExplanations: Lateral sacral arteries descend in front of the sacral plexus, they do not ascend across the pelvic inlet.
The superior gluteal artery passes posteriorly between the lumbosacral trunk and S1 to exit the pelvis; it does not ascend the inlet.
The deep circumflex iliac arises from the external iliac artery, not the internal iliac artery's posterior division.
The iliolumbar artery is unique among internal iliac branches for its recurrent/ascending course back toward the iliac fossa and lumbar region.
The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division and descends to exit the lower part of the greater sciatic foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Iliolumbar artery: this artery ascends across the pelvic inlet posterior to the external iliac vessels, psoas, and iliacus muscles.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Vascular Relationship: Uterine Artery and Ureter
statement: A 45-year-old woman undergoing total abdominal hysterectomy experiences significant bleeding near the lateral margin of the cervix. While attempting to ligate the uterine artery, the surgeon must be mindful of its specific relationship to the ureter. What is the most critical anatomical orientation of these structures at this site?
options: The uterine artery passes inferior to the ureter near the ischial spine.
The ureter crosses superiorly to the uterine artery within the broad ligament.
The uterine artery and ureter run parallel along the pelvic brim.
The uterine artery crosses superiorly to the ureter at the level of the internal os.
The uterine artery passes through the ureteric canal of the bladder wall.
correctOption: The uterine artery crosses superiorly to the ureter at the level of the internal os.
optionExplanations: The uterine artery passes superior to the ureter, often remembered by the mnemonic 'water under the bridge' (ureter is water, artery is the bridge).
This is the inverse of the actual relationship; the artery is superior and the ureter is inferior.
The structures are not parallel; they cross each other nearly at right angles in the base of the broad ligament.

As the uterine artery moves medially toward the cervix, it crosses the ureter superiorly at approximately the level of the internal os of the uterus. This is a high-risk area for ureteric injury during ligation.
The uterine artery does not enter the bladder wall; only the ureter pierces the bladder wall obliquely.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The uterine artery passes forward from the internal iliac artery and crosses the ureter at right angles to reach the cervix at the level of the internal os.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Drainage of the vaginal venous plexus
statement: A surgeon is performing a hysterectomy and notes a large venous plexus surrounding the vagina. Into which vessel does this vaginal venous plexus primarily drain?
optionExplanations: The external iliac vein primarily receives blood from the lower limb and abdominal wall.
The common iliac vein is formed by the union of internal and external veins; it is one step further in the circuit.
The inferior mesenteric vein is part of the portal system and drains the distal large bowel, not the vagina.
Like most pelvic viscera, the vagina's venous drainage eventually reaches the internal iliac vein through the vaginal venous plexus.
The IVC is the ultimate destination but the immediate drainage of the vaginal plexus is into the internal iliac system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The vaginal veins form a plexus around the vagina that drains into the internal iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A medical student is comparing the venous drainage patterns of the male and female gonads. Which physiological contrast is true regarding the termination of the gonadal veins?
options: The left gonadal vein joins the left renal vein
The left gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava
Both right and left gonadal veins drain into the internal iliac veins
The right gonadal vein joins the superior mesenteric vein
The right gonadal vein drains into the right renal vein
correctOption: The left gonadal vein joins the left renal vein
optionExplanations: The left testicular or ovarian vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, which is clinically significant for the development of varicoceles.
The left gonadal vein must first join the left renal vein because of the developmental asymmetry of the IVC.
The gonadal veins are abdominal vessels in their terminal course and do not drain into the internal iliac system.
There is no connection between the gonadal veins and the superior mesenteric vein, which belongs to the portal system.
The right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, unlike the left side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava on the right side and into the left renal vein on the left side.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Where does the external iliac vein begin its course?
options: Behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein
At the bifurcation of the common iliac vein
correctOption: Behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein
optionExplanations: The femoral vein changes its name to the external iliac vein at the moment it passes deep to the inguinal ligament to enter the pelvic cavity.
The ischioanal fossa contains the internal pudendal vessels and inferior rectal vessels, not the external iliac vein.
The prostatic venous plexus drains into the internal iliac vein, not the external iliac vein.
The bifurcation (or rather, union) of the internal and external iliac veins marks the *end* of these vessels and the start of the common iliac vein.
The internal iliac vein passes upward in front of the sacroiliac joint, but the external iliac vein begins at the inguinal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac vein begins behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
coreConcept: Terminal Branches of the Common Iliac Artery
statement: Which of the following is classified as a primary terminal branch of the common iliac artery?
optionExplanations: The deep circumflex iliac artery is a branch of the external iliac artery.
The median sacral artery is a small branch arising from the aorta at its bifurcation, not from the common iliac artery itself.
The common iliac artery divides into two terminal branches: the internal iliac artery (which enters the true pelvis) and the external iliac artery (which follows the pelvic brim).
The inferior epigastric artery is a branch of the external iliac artery, not the common iliac.
The obturator artery is usually a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Each common iliac artery ends at the pelvic inlet in front of the sacroiliac joint by dividing into the external and internal iliac arteries (see Figs. 8.10 and 8.18).

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A 68-year-old male with confirmed prostatic carcinoma presents with new-onset lumbar spine pain. Pelvic imaging suggests skeletal metastasis. Which pelvic venous structure provides the anatomical pathway for cancer cells to reach the vertebral column without passing through the lungs?
options: The prostatic venous plexus and its connections to the vertebral veins
correctOption: The prostatic venous plexus and its connections to the vertebral veins
optionExplanations: The prostatic venous plexus is valveless and communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus. Changes in abdominal pressure can cause retrograde flow, allowing prostatic cancer cells to bypass the IVC and lodge in the vertebrae.
The internal pudendal vein drains the perineum and lower anal canal; while it drains to the internal iliac, it is not the primary route for vertebral metastasis from the prostate.
The deep circumflex iliac vein drains the iliac fossa and is unrelated to the drainage of the prostate or the vertebral plexus.
The external iliac vein drains the lower limb and does not have the direct valveless connections to the vertebral column seen with the pelvic plexuses.
The inferior epigastric vein drains the anterior abdominal wall into the external iliac vein and is not involved in this metastatic pathway.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Many connections exist between the prostatic venous plexus and the vertebral veins. During coughing and sneezing... it is possible for prostatic venous blood to flow in a reverse direction and enter the vertebral veins.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: During a gynecological procedure, a surgeon identifies a venous plexus surrounding the vagina. This plexus eventually drains into which of the following larger vessels?
optionExplanations: The internal iliac vein is the primary vessel for the venous return of the true pelvis, receiving blood from plexuses surrounding the bladder, prostate, uterus, and vagina.
The vaginal veins drain into the internal iliac vein first; they do not join the IVC directly.
The superior mesenteric vein drains the midgut and is part of the portal system, unrelated to the vaginal venous return.
The common iliac vein is the destination for the internal iliac vein, but the vaginal plexus specifically terminates in the internal iliac.
The external iliac vein does not drain the pelvic viscera; it is primarily for the lower limb and abdominal wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The vaginal veins form a plexus around the vagina that drains into the internal iliac vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: Which abdominal vessel crosses the external iliac artery at the pelvic inlet to reach its destination in the female pelvis?
optionExplanations: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and crosses the common iliac, not the external iliac at the inlet.
The uterine artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery and does not cross the external iliac artery at the pelvic inlet; it stays within the true pelvis.
The obturator artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery and remains medial to the external iliac system.
The ovarian artery originates from the abdominal aorta at L1. As it descends to enter the pelvis, it must cross over the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim to reach the suspensory ligament.
The middle rectal artery is a branch of the internal iliac and arises within the true pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal part of the aorta... It crosses the external iliac artery at the pelvic inlet and enters the suspensory ligament of the ovary.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
coreConcept: Divisions of the Internal Iliac Artery
statement: Which of the following vessels is accurately classified as a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
optionExplanations: The internal iliac artery splits into anterior and posterior divisions. The posterior division typically gives rise to the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries.
The obturator artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
The middle rectal artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
The umbilical artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
The inferior gluteal artery is a branch of the anterior division, distinguishing it from the superior gluteal artery which is posterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Posterior Division Branches... Superior gluteal artery: this artery leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle. It supplies the gluteal region.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Varicocele as a Sign of Renal Malignancy
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with a rapidly developing left-sided varicocele and microscopic hematuria. On examination, the varicocele does not decompress when supine. Based on the venous anatomy of the pelvis and abdomen, which structure must be urgently evaluated?
options: The prostate gland for enlargement obstructing the internal iliac vein
The left kidney for malignant disease extending into the renal vein
The right testis for synchronous bilateral testicular torsion
The urinary bladder for a tumor obstructing the vesical plexus
The sigmoid colon for a volvulus compressing the common iliac vein
correctOption: The left kidney for malignant disease extending into the renal vein
optionExplanations: Prostatic enlargement affects the prostatic urethra or bladder neck, not the superiorly located renal/testicular venous junction.
Since the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, any obstruction of the renal vein (such as by a renal cell carcinoma thrombus) will cause secondary varicocele.
Testicular torsion is an arterial/rotation emergency and does not present as a non-decompressing varicocele.
The vesical plexus drains the bladder and does not influence the pressure within the pampiniform plexus/testicular vein.
Sigmoid volvulus presents with bowel obstruction symptoms; while it could theoretically compress veins, the specific anatomic link for varicocele is the renal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Rarely, malignant disease of the left kidney extends along the renal vein and blocks the exit of the testicular vein. A rapidly developing left-sided varicocele should therefore always lead one to examine the left kidney.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
coreConcept: Origin of the external iliac vein
statement: In the pelvic venous system, which vessel is a direct continuation of the femoral vein after it passes deep to the inguinal ligament?
optionExplanations: The internal pudendal vein drains the perineum and is a tributary of the internal iliac vein.
The internal iliac vein begins from visceral and parietal tributaries within the true pelvis.
The external iliac vein is the name given to the venous trunk once it leaves the thigh and enters the pelvis by passing behind the inguinal ligament.
The common iliac vein is formed by the union of the internal and external iliac veins.
The inferior epigastric vein is a tributary that joins the external iliac vein; it is not the main trunk continuation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The external iliac vein begins behind the inguinal ligament as a continuation of the femoral vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of common iliac artery
statement: In the context of the vascular course within the pelvis, what is the precise relationship between the common iliac artery and the ureter at the pelvic brim?
options: The ureter runs medial and parallel to the artery without crossing
The ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the artery
The artery crosses anterior to the mid-portion of the ureter
The artery and ureter enter the pelvis through the obturator canal
The ureter passes posterior to the common iliac artery
correctOption: The ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the artery
optionExplanations: The ureter does not simply run parallel; it must enter the pelvis by crossing the major vascular bifurcation at the brim.

This is a critical anatomical relationship often described as 'water under the bridge' (though that specific phrase refers to the uterine artery, the ureter crossing the iliac bifurcation is the initial pelvic landmark).
The text explicitly states the ureter crosses the artery, not the reverse, as the ureter descends from the kidney to the bladder.
Neither the common iliac nor the ureter enters the obturator canal; the obturator canal contains the obturator nerve and vessels.
The ureter is a retroperitoneal structure that stays anterior to the major vascular bifurcation at the sacroiliac joint to enter the true pelvis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery in front of the sacroiliac joint

category: Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of external and internal iliac arteries
statement: The internal iliac artery typically divides into its anterior and posterior divisions at which specific anatomical location?
options: Level of the pelvic brim medial to the ureter
Behind the middle of the sacroiliac joint
At the level of the ischial spine
At the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen
correctOption: At the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen
optionExplanations: The pelvic brim is the level of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, not the site where the internal iliac divides into divisions.
While the internal iliac artery begins in front of the sacroiliac joint, its division occurs lower at the sciatic foramen margin.
The inguinal ligament is the landmark for the transition of the external iliac artery to the femoral artery, and is not related to the internal iliac divisions.
The ischial spine is a landmark for the ureter's turn and the crossing of the internal pudendal nerve, but the internal iliac divisions are formed superior to this.
The anatomical landmark for the bifurcation of the internal iliac artery into its two main divisions is the superior border of the greater sciatic foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The internal iliac artery passes down into the pelvis to the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen, where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions (see Fig. 8.10).

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: A 20-year-old male presents with a rapidly developing left-sided varicocele. On physical examination, the clinician notes a 'bag of worms' appearance in the left scrotum. Why must the clinician perform a thorough examination of the left kidney in this specific scenario?
options: The left testicular vein joins the left renal vein where pressure is higher than the IVC
The right testicular vein joins the high-pressure left renal vein
The left testicular vein drains directly into the internal iliac vein near the kidney
Malignant renal disease typically obstructs the inferior vena cava directly
The left renal vein is a low-pressure vessel compared to the right renal vein
correctOption: The left testicular vein joins the left renal vein where pressure is higher than the IVC
optionExplanations: The left testicular vein's drainage into the left renal vein makes it susceptible to obstruction by renal masses or increased pressure, explaining why left-sided varicoceles are more common and potentially indicative of renal pathology.
The right testicular vein joins the inferior vena cava, not the renal vein.
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, not the internal iliac vein.
While renal disease can obstruct the IVC, the specific clinical correlation for a left varicocele is the obstruction of the left renal vein.
The text states the pressure is higher in the left renal vein compared to the low-pressure inferior vena cava where the right side drains.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": This is thought to be because the right testicular vein joins the low-pressure inferior vena cava, whereas the left vein joins the left renal vein, in which the venous pressure is higher. Rarely, malignant disease of the left kidney extends along the renal vein and blocks the exit of the testicular vein.

category: Describe the origin, course, tributaries and area of drainage of pelvic veins
statement: Which of the following describes the correct sequence of venous flow from the deep dorsal vein of the penis into the systemic circulation?
options: Deep dorsal vein → Internal pudendal vein → Inferior vena cava
Deep dorsal vein → External iliac vein → Common iliac vein
Deep dorsal vein → Vesical plexus → External iliac vein
Deep dorsal vein → Femoral vein → Common iliac vein
Deep dorsal vein → Prostatic venous plexus → Internal iliac vein
correctOption: Deep dorsal vein → Prostatic venous plexus → Internal iliac vein
optionExplanations: While the internal pudendal vein drains the superficial structures of the penis, the deep dorsal vein specifically enters the prostatic plexus.
The deep dorsal vein does not drain into the external iliac system; it enters the pelvic cavity through the urogenital hiatus.
